about: The test set for G2, the meaning check (lib/learning/judge.ts). Each group is a SOURCE as the reader sees it (passages and a code example); each case is one sentence of an AI explanation under it, with the verdict a careful reader gives: 'flag' when it contradicts the source or states a technical fact the source does not support, 'ok' otherwise (analogies and plain definitions are allowed). 'line' marks a walk-through sentence and the code line it explains. scripts/eval-judge.mjs sends every group to the real judge (it costs 20b tokens; it is not part of npm test).

passages: The interpreter acts as a simple calculator: you can type an expression into it and it will write the value. Expression syntax is straightforward: the operators +, -, * and / can be used to perform arithmetic; parentheses (()) can be used for grouping.
source.code:
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> 50 - 5*6
20
>>> (50 - 5*6) / 4
5.0
>>> 8 / 5  # division always returns a floating-point number
1.6

cases.found: first live lesson, 2026-10-10: the old judge passed it
cases.sentence: Parentheses tell Python which parts to calculate first.
cases.why: the source only says parentheses are for grouping; the order of calculation is a new technical claim

cases.sentence: You can use +, -, * and / to do arithmetic, and parentheses to group parts of it.
Think of the interpreter as a pocket calculator that waits for you to type a sum.
An expression is a small piece of arithmetic, such as 2 + 2, that has a value.
cases.why: a plain definition that agrees with the source

cases.sentence: Here you ask Python to add 2 and 2, and it writes the value 4 on the next line.
Dividing 8 by 5 gives 1.6, because division always returns a floating-point number.
cases.why: the code's own comment and output say so

cases.sentence: Dividing one whole number by another always gives a whole number.
The interpreter checks your whole program for mistakes before it runs any of it.
cases.why: a claim about how the interpreter works that the source does not make

cases.sentence: Python is one of the fastest languages for arithmetic.
Python works this out and saves the answer in a variable called result.
cases.why: the code shows the value; nothing stores it

passages: The equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable. Afterwards, no result is displayed before the next interactive prompt:

cases.sentence: The equal sign gives the name width the value 20.
Python shows nothing after this line; it just remembers the value.
cases.why: the passage says no result is displayed

cases.sentence: A variable is a value that can never change once it is set.
cases.why: a technical claim the source does not support

cases.sentence: Variables also make your programs run faster.
So the equal sign gives a name a value that later lines can use.
cases.why: line 3 uses width and height again
